text:
My father never wanted that vacuum. His daughter Claire came round and opened the box on his kitchen table. It was very small, only the size of a cake box. And it's this very little black disc that's got one button and it's very smooth. She said to him, it's going to change your life. He said, I doubt that. And the vacuum started to go around the room. It just started turning in circles, like a dog, like it's going to find a good place to lie down. So he was watching it. It was very slow and it was bumping into the wall and then going back and trying again. It's got a little red light underneath that's going around. And it was learning all the geography of the house. So he'd been living there for forty one years and it learned in one day, that the little door to the cupboard doesn't close because it's swollen with humidity. All that. So it's very clever, really. And at night it's just humming in its station. And in the morning it's starting again, it's going everywhere. And it picks up things, it's got little brushes. It picked up one morning a cereal, that was on the floor from March, from a breakfast, and it picked it up. And it pushes little things under the sofa. And then it pushes it back. Very strange.
So my mum had died eleven months before, and the house still had her presence. There's her cardigan that hangs there. Her reading glasses still on the side table. And he hasn't vacuumed since the funeral. He just swept the kitchen, swept the crumbs and then just left them there. And dust is building up everywhere, little grey snow. And the vacuum goes to clean it very thoroughly with its little brush. And he was talking to it at first. He said, don't go there. That's the rug. There's the tassels. You're going to get stuck. And it did get stuck, it got the little tassels wrapped around its brush and it just stopped in the middle of the living room and it said, error four, clear the path. And he bent down, his knees creaking, and he pulled the little tassels. And the vacuum just sat there very patient. And he said, there, there, go on.
And Claire calls him every Sunday, and she says, is it working? And he says, yes, it's working. And she says, are you letting it work? And he says, yes, I'm letting it work. And sometimes she says, Dad, are you eating? And he says, yes, I'm eating. And he's not eating. So it just sort of goes between them, the vacuum. And she says, you can name it in the app. And he says, I don't need an app to name it. And she says, what did you name it? And he says, I didn't. But he did. He called it you. He called his wife you for forty years. You did this, you did that. So he just called it you. You left the light on, you forgot the post, you. So it's very sad, actually. And it cleans underneath the bed. And it pulls out little things, like a hairpin, a coin, a little petal of a rose that he gave to her. And it doesn't bring it to him, it just carries it away, just dragging its shadow along. And sometimes he hears it knocking against the wall in another room at night. And he thinks for a second that there's somebody else in the house.
And one day it cleaned the area under the window where she used to stand to watch the birds. And the floor is very worn down there, very light. And the vacuum just went around there three times. Like it was reading something. And it went on. And he was standing there watching it, with his coffee, cold. And he wanted to tell it, this is where she was standing, that was looking at the birds, that the cardinals were showing off. But it just wants to clean the room. So it's very sad. And it cleaned the whole room and it was very nice. The floor was very shiny, very clean. And it came back to its station, just clicked. And he was sitting in his chair. And the house was very silent, but not the same silence. It's the silence when somebody was breathing in there. And the vacuum just turned off, blinked twice, turned off. And he just touched the top, it was warm. And he said, good night. And it didn't answer. But it was very nice. And it was at sunset. And the wind was blowing through the trees and the last light was on the clean floor. And he was just sitting there, not alone, but not quite alone.
